title: Indian Society: Suggestions for Project Work

topics.title: Choosing a method: surveys, interviews, observation

learn.hook: Want to know how many students in your school use the metro? Ask a hundred of them. Want to know how it feels to be the only girl in a physics tuition batch? Sit down and talk to a few. Different questions need different methods.
points: This chapter is non-evaluative in the CBSE 2026-27 theory paper, but it supports the 20-mark project. Its purpose is to give you first-hand experience of doing a small piece of sociological research.
The research question decides the method. There is no single 'best' method; each suits some questions better than others.
Survey: collecting the same information from many people, often with a questionnaire (a fixed list of written questions). Good for patterns and numbers.
Interview: a conversation with a respondent. Structured interviews follow fixed questions; open-ended (unstructured) interviews let the respondent talk freely and give depth.
Observation: participant observation (the researcher joins in the activity being studied) or non-participant observation (the researcher watches without taking part).

example.q: Which method suits each question? (a) What share of Class 12 students use coaching? (b) How do domestic workers experience their employers' homes? (c) How do people use a bus stop at rush hour?
steps: (a) Needs numbers from many people: survey with a questionnaire.
(b) Needs depth and feelings: open-ended interviews.

learn.reallife: Organisations like the NSSO run giant surveys of lakhs of households, while journalists often use long interviews; your project can borrow either style on a small scale.

games.title: Best method for the question
items: How many families own a two-wheeler?
What percentage of students walk to school?

quiz.q: The main purpose of the project work chapter is to:
options: Teach statistical formulas and nothing else at all
Replace the whole theory syllabus with projects
Give first-hand experience of small-scale research
Train students to work as government census officers
quiz.explain: It introduces students to doing research themselves.

quiz.q: What decides which research method to use?
options: The research question
The researcher's favourite method
The cheapest method
The method used last year
quiz.explain: Methods are chosen to fit the question.

quiz.q: A survey is best suited for:
options: Studying one person's life story in great depth
Collecting the same information from many people
Joining a group's daily activities for months
Reading old letters kept in an archive
quiz.explain: Surveys gather comparable data across many respondents.
quiz.mistake: Confuses survey with interview or observation

quiz.q: In participant observation, the researcher:
options: Only reads documents and old records
Sends written questionnaires by post
Watches from a hidden camera only
Takes part in the activity being studied
quiz.explain: The researcher joins in to understand from inside.

quiz.q: An open-ended interview is useful because it:
options: Lets respondents explain in their own words
Uses only short yes-or-no questions
Gives quick numbers for very large groups
Needs no conversation with anyone at all
quiz.explain: It yields depth and meaning.
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with a structured questionnaire

quiz.q: Which is a non-participant observation?
options: Working a week as a tea-stall helper to study it
Watching how commuters board a crowded bus
Joining a dance troupe to study it
Playing in a local cricket team to study it
quiz.explain: The researcher only watches, without joining.
quiz.mistake: Picks examples where the researcher participates

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): There is no single best method in sociology.
Reason (R): Different research questions call for different methods.
options: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R explains A
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Because questions differ, the right method differs.
quiz.mistake: Thinks one method is always superior

quiz.q: The CBSE Sociology project carries how many marks?
quiz.explain: The project is worth 20 marks; the theory paper 80.

teach.ask: Gappu holds a clipboard: 'I want to research my school canteen. Should I do a survey, an interview or just watch?'
teach.praise: So the question decides the method: surveys for numbers, interviews for depth, observation for behaviour. Clipboard ready!
teach.nudge: But how do I choose between methods? What does each one do best?

topics.title: Other sources, mixed methods, ethics and the project file

learn.hook: An old family wedding album can tell you how dress, guests and rituals have changed over 50 years. Sociologists use photographs, letters, newspapers and records as data too.
points: Archives, old documents, photographs, letters, newspapers and other media are valuable sources, especially for studying change over time.
Combining methods (mixed methods), such as a survey plus a few interviews, gives a fuller picture than any single method.
Ethics: get informed consent, respect privacy and confidentiality, avoid harm, and treat respondents with respect. Never publish names or details without permission.
A project report usually has: introduction, statement of purpose, research question, methodology (methods and sample), data analysis, and conclusion.
The project is followed by a viva voce, an oral discussion where you explain what you did and what you found.

example.q: Arrange the parts of a project report in a sensible order.
example.answer: Introduction → purpose → question → methodology → analysis → conclusion.

learn.reallife: Many families have photos from the 1970s onwards; comparing them with today's wedding photos is a quick, ethical archive project, as long as you have permission to use them.

games.title: Project report

games.title: Research ethics
items: A researcher should take consent before interviewing someone.
Informed consent is a basic ethical rule.
It is fine to publish a respondent's private details without asking.
Privacy and confidentiality must be respected.
Old photographs can be used as sociological data.
They show change over time.
Using two methods together can give a fuller picture.
That is the strength of mixed methods.
The viva voce is a written test on the textbook.
It is an oral discussion based on the project.

quiz.q: Which source is most useful for studying how wedding customs changed over 50 years?
options: A survey of this year's weddings only
Old photographs and wedding invitations
A single interview with a child
Today's weather report
quiz.explain: Archival materials show change over time.
quiz.mistake: Picks a source limited to the present

quiz.q: 'Mixed methods' means:
options: Mixing up answers from respondents
Using no method at all
Combining two or more research methods
Copying another student's data
quiz.explain: Combining methods gives a fuller picture.

quiz.q: Informed consent means:
options: The researcher decides on behalf of the respondent
The respondent agrees after knowing the study's purpose
The teacher signs on behalf of all respondents
No one is told anything about the study
quiz.explain: Respondents must understand and agree.

quiz.q: Which is an ethical practice in research?
options: Keeping respondents' identities confidential
Publishing names without any permission
Recording people secretly without consent
Changing answers to suit the hypothesis
quiz.explain: Confidentiality protects respondents.

quiz.q: Which section of a project explains how data were collected?
options: Conclusion
Introduction
Bibliography
Methodology
quiz.explain: Methodology describes methods and sample.

quiz.q: The viva voce in project assessment is:
options: An oral discussion based on the project
A written test on the whole textbook
A group dance performance on stage
A multiple-choice exam on the syllabus
quiz.explain: It is an oral examination on the project.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Combining a survey with interviews can strengthen a project.
Reason (R): Surveys show patterns, while interviews explain meanings.
options: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R explains A
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Each method fills gaps left by the other.

quiz.q: Which part of a project states what you finally found?
options: Conclusion
Statement of purpose
Research question
Methodology
quiz.explain: The conclusion sums up findings.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Can I use old photos as data? And what goes into a project file?'
teach.praise: Old photos count! Mix methods, take consent, and write intro, purpose, question, methods, analysis and conclusion. Then the viva!
teach.nudge: But what other sources can I use, and what ethics must I follow?

learn.hook: Who gets to sit on the bench at a bus stop? Who cooks and who washes up at home? Who appears on the front page of the newspaper? Everyday life is full of research questions.
points: Public use of space: who uses streets, parks, bus stops and markets, at what times, and how gender, age and class shape their use.
Media: how the content of newspapers or television has changed over time, e.g. which topics and groups get coverage.
Households and domestic work: who does what at home, and how the division of labour is gendered.
Transport: modes of travel (walking, cycle, bus, metro, car) and their social aspects, such as cost, safety and who uses which mode.

Life histories of people, places or everyday objects (e.g. the life of a cycle-rickshaw puller, a neighbourhood, or the pressure cooker). Students may also choose other local themes linked to the book.

example.q: Design a mini-project on domestic work in your neighbourhood.
steps: Question: who does cooking, cleaning and child care in 20 households?
Method: a short survey plus two open-ended interviews.
Ethics: take consent; do not record names.
Analysis: compare tasks done by men, women and children; draw a conclusion.
example.answer: A clear question, suitable methods, ethics and analysis make a sound project.

learn.reallife: Delhi Metro's women-only coaches and the debate around them are a ready-made project theme on gender and public space.

quiz.q: A project on who uses a park at different times studies:
options: Household domestic work
Media content over time
Public use of space
Life histories of objects
quiz.explain: It is about how public space is used.

quiz.q: Comparing newspaper front pages from 1990 and today is a project on:
options: Media
Transport
Domestic work
Public use of space
quiz.explain: It traces change in media content.

quiz.q: Studying the gendered division of chores at home falls under:
options: Public use of space and streets
Transport and modes of travel
Households and domestic work
Media and changes in its content
quiz.explain: It is about domestic labour.

quiz.q: A study of why people choose buses, autos or the metro is about:
options: Transport
Domestic work
Media
Life histories
quiz.explain: It examines modes of travel and their social aspects.

quiz.q: A 'life history' project could focus on:
options: How the use of a pressure cooker changed over decades
The weather forecast issued for the city for today
The final score of a single day's cricket match
One random post that was seen on social media
quiz.explain: Life histories can trace people, places or objects over time.

quiz.q: Why is 'public use of space' a sociological theme?
options: Space has no social meaning whatsoever
Only architects are allowed to study space
Use of space is shaped by gender, age and class
Everyone uses space in exactly the same way
quiz.explain: Who uses which spaces, and when, reveals social patterns.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Students may choose local themes beyond those listed.
Reason (R): Projects can be linked to any topic of the book.
options: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R explains A
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: The list is suggestive, not exhaustive.
quiz.mistake: Thinks only listed themes are allowed

quiz.q: Which is the best research question for a transport project?
options: How do cost and safety shape women's travel choices?
What colour are the city buses in our town?
How many wheels does an auto-rickshaw have?
In which year was the first motor car invented?
quiz.explain: A good question links transport to social factors.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What topics can I pick for my sociology project? Something from daily life?'
teach.praise: So I can study streets, media, housework, transport or life histories, or any local theme linked to the book. Project, here I come!
teach.nudge: But which themes does the book suggest, and how do they connect to sociology?
